blocks.content: The previous topic covered the OSI model's seven layers, a complete map for talking about networking one layer at a time. If that made sense, you already have the mental shelf space this topic needs, because everything here fits onto the exact same shelf, just organized differently.

Here is the direct answer to a question worth asking early: OSI is mostly a teaching and troubleshooting tool. The model the real internet is actually built on, the one every protocol you use today maps onto, is called TCP/IP, and that is the entire subject of this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784012607041-987317675.png
blocks.alt: OSI is mostly a teaching model, TCP/IP is what the real internet actually runs on

blocks.content: 1. Where TCP/IP Came From

TCP/IP takes its name from its two most famous protocols: Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol. Put those two names together and you get the model's own name, a small hint at how practical this model has always been. It was named after what it actually does, not after some abstract design goal.

It was developed for ARPANET, the United States government funded research network that is the internet's direct ancestor. TCP/IP was not sketched on a whiteboard and handed to engineers to implement afterward. It grew directly out of the process of building and running an actual, working, growing network, refined by real traffic and real failures along the way.

That history matters because it explains everything else in this topic. This is not an abstract theoretical exercise you learn once and set aside. This model is how the real internet works, right now, carrying the exact request that loaded this very page onto your screen.

blocks.title: Also called the Internet Protocol Suite
blocks.content: TCP/IP is a nickname. In formal documents you will sometimes see it called the Internet Protocol Suite, but almost everyone, including this course, just calls it TCP/IP after its two most famous protocols.
2. The Four Layers, Bottom to Top
blocks.text: 2. The Four Layers, Bottom to Top

blocks.content: TCP/IP organizes everything into four layers instead of OSI's seven. Do not read that as TCP/IP being a simplified or dumbed down version of OSI. It is more accurate to say TCP/IP groups related responsibilities together into fewer, coarser layers, because in practice some of OSI's boundaries never mattered enough on their own to justify being separate layers in a working system.

Like OSI, TCP/IP is read from the bottom up: the layer closest to the physical wire sits at the bottom, and the layer closest to you, the one your browser or app actually talks to, sits at the top. Each layer wraps the data handed to it by the layer above, adds its own information, and passes it down to the layer below. Every layer only needs to understand its direct neighbours, not the whole stack at once, and that single rule is what keeps the whole system maintainable.

blocks.title: Protocol Data Units have their own names
blocks.content: Each layer wraps data in its own container with its own name: a segment at the Transport layer, a packet at the Internet layer, a frame at the Network Access layer. The worked example near the end of this topic walks through all of them in order.
3. Layer One: The Network Access Layer
blocks.text: 3. Layer One: The Network Access Layer

blocks.content: The Network Access layer, sometimes just called the Link layer, sits at the very bottom of the stack. It combines what OSI splits into two separate layers, Physical and Data Link, into one single practical layer. Its job in one sentence: get data onto the actual physical medium and handle communication with whatever device is directly connected to you.

This is the layer where Ethernet and WiFi live. Ethernet defines how bits travel down a physical cable between devices on the same local network, and WiFi defines the same idea over radio waves instead of copper. Both handle framing the data, catching basic transmission errors, and using hardware addresses, MAC addresses, to identify devices sharing the same local link.

Notice what this layer does not do: it has no idea what network it is part of, and no idea where data is ultimately headed beyond the next directly connected device. That job belongs entirely to the layer above it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784012610899-354183878.png
blocks.alt: The Network Access layer: Ethernet or WiFi moving data between devices on the same local network

blocks.content: 4. Layer Two: The Internet Layer

The Internet layer maps directly onto OSI's Network layer, no combining, no splitting, a clean one to one match. This is the layer where IP addressing and routing between different networks happens, and the Internet Protocol itself, IP, lives here.

Every device on a network gets an IP address, and every packet at this layer carries a source address and a destination address. Routers operate at this layer: they read the destination IP address on each packet and decide which direction to forward it, hopping the packet from network to network until it reaches the one the destination lives on.

This is also the layer where the Network Access layer's local, directly connected view expands into a global one. A single WiFi frame only knows about the device next to it; an IP packet at the Internet layer can be addressed to a server on the other side of the planet.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784012612650-358499297.png

blocks.content: 5. Layer Three: The Transport Layer

The Transport layer also maps directly onto OSI's Transport layer, another clean one to one match. Its job is end to end delivery, not just between two machines, but between the correct applications running on those two machines. TCP and UDP both live here.

This is the layer that introduces ports, the numbers that identify a specific application on a device, so a web browser's traffic and an email client's traffic on the same laptop never get mixed up even though they share the same IP address. TCP adds reliability on top of that: it tracks what has arrived, requests anything missing, and puts data back in order. UDP skips that overhead and just sends, trading reliability for speed.

Whether a connection uses TCP or UDP is a Transport layer decision, made independently of what the Internet layer below it and the Application layer above it are doing. Web pages typically ride on TCP for reliability; live video calls often ride on UDP because a slightly dropped frame matters less than a delayed one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784012614295-562388010.png

blocks.content: 6. Layer Four: The Application Layer

The Application layer sits at the top of the stack, and it is the biggest simplification TCP/IP makes compared to OSI. It combines three separate OSI layers, Session, Presentation, and Application, into one single practical layer, because in real systems those distinctions rarely needed to be separate layers at all.

Every application protocol you use daily lives here: HTTP for web pages, DNS for translating names into IP addresses, SMTP for email, FTP for file transfer. This is the layer closest to you, the one that actually understands what the data means, a webpage, an email, a file, rather than just moving bytes around.

Formatting, encoding, and session management, the jobs OSI hands to Presentation and Session separately, are simply handled inside whichever application protocol needs them, instead of living in their own dedicated layers. HTTP, for example, handles its own formatting and its own notion of a session without needing help from a layer underneath it.

blocks.title: The mapping is not perfectly even
blocks.content: Notice the split is not even. TCP/IP squeezes three OSI layers, Session, Presentation, and Application, into one single Application layer, and it squeezes two OSI layers, Data Link and Physical, into one single Network Access layer. Only Transport and Internet map one to one.
8. Why TCP/IP Won, and Why You Still Need OSI Too
blocks.text: 8. Why TCP/IP Won, and Why You Still Need OSI Too

blocks.content: TCP/IP won as the practical standard for a simple reason: it was built and battle tested by actually running the early internet, ARPANET, while OSI was designed by a standards committee as a more abstract, complete reference model. TCP/IP shipped, carried real traffic, and got refined by real failures. OSI was still being finalized on paper while TCP/IP was already connecting real machines.

In practice, engineers needed something that shipped and worked, not something theoretically perfect. By the time OSI was ready as a complete standard, TCP/IP already had a running network, real adoption, and real momentum behind it. That head start is the entire story of why one model became the internet and the other became a diagram in a textbook.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784012619227-159998906.png
blocks.alt: TCP/IP was refined by running a real network; OSI was finished on paper after TCP/IP already had adoption

None of that makes OSI worthless though. OSI gives you precise troubleshooting vocabulary, being able to say this is a layer 3 problem or this is a layer 2 problem pins down exactly where in the stack something is failing. TCP/IP gives you the model that maps onto what you actually build and debug day to day. The rest of this course builds entirely on TCP/IP's layer names: Transport layer topics, Internet layer topics like IP addressing, and Application layer topics like HTTP are all still ahead of you.

blocks.title: Speaking both languages at work
blocks.content: When a colleague says this looks like a layer 3 problem, they are using OSI's numbering, layer 3 is the Network layer, even though the system in front of them is built on TCP/IP. That cross vocabulary is completely normal in the industry, and now you can follow both sides of the conversation.
9. Tracing a Web Request Through All Four Layers
blocks.text: 9. Tracing a Web Request Through All Four Layers

blocks.content: The cleanest way to make all four layers concrete at once is to trace one single web request all the way down the stack and back up. Say your browser wants to load a webpage.

The Application layer wraps that request in an HTTP request, addressed to a specific resource on a specific server. The Transport layer wraps that HTTP request inside a TCP segment, attaching port numbers and the tracking information that guarantees reliable delivery. The Internet layer wraps that segment inside an IP packet, stamping it with the source and destination IP addresses needed to route it across the internet. The Network Access layer takes that packet and puts it onto the actual wire or radio signal as raw bits, the only form data can travel in physically.

The receiving server does the exact same process in reverse. Its Network Access layer reads the bits off the wire, its Internet layer strips off the IP packet to confirm it arrived at the right destination, its Transport layer strips off the TCP segment and reassembles things in order, and its Application layer finally hands a clean HTTP request to the web server software, which can now actually respond.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784012620748-411986853.png

10. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways
A couple of misunderstandings come up constantly once TCP/IP and OSI sit side by side, and both are worth naming directly.

["Assuming TCP/IP has exactly the same seven layers as OSI, just renamed. It does not. TCP/IP genuinely combines several OSI layers together into fewer, coarser layers: three OSI layers become one Application layer, and two OSI layers become one Network Access layer.","Assuming OSI is what real systems actually implement, when TCP/IP is the actual practical model running underneath. OSI is the vocabulary you reach for while troubleshooting, TCP/IP is the model the protocols themselves are built on.","Mixing up layer numbers between the two models. OSI's Network layer is layer 3; TCP/IP's Internet layer does the identical job, but TCP/IP diagrams do not always number layers the same way OSI does, so match by name, not just by number."]
items: Assuming TCP/IP has exactly the same seven layers as OSI, just renamed. It does not. TCP/IP genuinely combines several OSI layers together into fewer, coarser layers: three OSI layers become one Application layer, and two OSI layers become one Network Access layer.

Assuming OSI is what real systems actually implement, when TCP/IP is the actual practical model running underneath. OSI is the vocabulary you reach for while troubleshooting, TCP/IP is the model the protocols themselves are built on.

Mixing up layer numbers between the two models. OSI's Network layer is layer 3; TCP/IP's Internet layer does the identical job, but TCP/IP diagrams do not always number layers the same way OSI does, so match by name, not just by number.
